title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: New statewide map tracks 20+ data center proposals and their stakes for bills, water and towns.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy. We're kicking off this Monday with the latest tracker showing more than 20 active proposals from Monroe up to the Upper Peninsula, all chasing cheap power.
Exactly. That new weekly roundup from Michigan Advance and Crain's Detroit lays out every site with power deals, tax incentives, or local pushback already in play.
Why does this map matter so much right now? Residents 30 miles away are already connecting the dots to higher electric rates and new transmission lines.

The bigger picture is the scale of the boom. Michigan's relatively affordable power and available land have drawn developers hard, but every gigawatt-scale project pulls from the same grid and water sources.
Walk me through the history here. How long has this tension been building?

It's accelerated in the last couple years as AI and cloud demand exploded nationally. Michigan saw early proposals in metro Detroit suburbs and west Michigan, then it spread to mid-state counties and now the U.P.
Who are the main players? Developers, utilities, or the towns themselves?

It's a mix. Development firms secure the sites and tax breaks, utilities like Consumers or DTE handle the grid connections, and local officials decide on zoning and incentives. Residents are the ones showing up at meetings with questions about bills and noise.
What does this mean for electric bills if even a handful move forward?
The tracker notes that new infrastructure costs often get socialized across ratepayers. People far from any site could still see increases to cover transmission upgrades and capacity additions.
Water is another big one. These facilities need massive cooling. How does that play out in rural areas?

Exactly. Proposals near rivers or lakes raise red flags about drawdown and discharge. Some sites are looking at closed-loop systems, but locals still worry about long-term strain on aquifers and farmland irrigation.
And farmland conversion? That's been a flashpoint in other states.

Yes. Prime agricultural land gets rezoned for these campuses, which can mean lost tax base for schools or permanent changes to the rural character. The tracker flags which projects already have incentives locked in.
What happens next with so many proposals in play?

More public hearings, possible moratoria like the one being debated in St. Joseph County, and lawsuits testing how far towns can push back. The Gibraltar case is already heading to court over a year-long pause.
That sounds like it could set precedents statewide.
It could. If the developer wins in Gibraltar, other cities might hesitate on pauses. If the city holds, it strengthens local control arguments.
Any early signs which sites are furthest along?
The map highlights those with grid connections or tax deals secured. Mason County's project just had the developer named, and GenH is pitching Morley Dam in Mecosta as a self-powered option.
Self-powered could sidestep some utility fights, but still hits water and local services.
Right. Commissioners in Mason County already flagged impacts on EMS, roads, and budgets. Similar talks are happening in townships across the state.
This feels like the start of a longer statewide conversation.
It does. The tracker is updated weekly, so we'll keep watching which proposals advance and where the pushback lands.
Let's move to quick hits. Yesterday Mason County weighed how data centers could hit local services.
Commissioners there discussed EMS, roads, and budget trade-offs. Rural residents would face higher power loads if projects move ahead.
Also yesterday, GenH floated using Morley Dam in Mecosta County for on-site power generation.
That approach might avoid some grid fights but still raises water-use questions under state rules.
Shifting to Saturday, a township rejected a server farm on Kluver Road after noise, traffic, and water concerns.
Officials turned down the permit, keeping that rural area free of large-scale facilities for now.
South Haven residents are also fighting rezoning on Baseline property for similar reasons.
The opposition there could influence nearby western Michigan townships facing the same decisions.
In the U.P., Forsyth residents grilled officials on power rates, water, and rumored military ties.
Hundreds showed up in Marquette County for their first direct look at the scale of proposals.
And a developer is suing Gibraltar to overturn its year-long moratorium.
The case tests how far local governments can go to slow these power-hungry projects.
Friday brought news that the firm behind the Mason project is now named.
Ingham County residents have a clearer target for questions on water, noise, and grid effects.
St. Joseph County is weighing a two-year freeze while it studies impacts.
That decision could influence other southwest Michigan townships worried about bills and lost farmland.
Now for on deck. What meetings can listeners actually attend today and tomorrow?
Today Lyon Township Planning Commission takes up Project Flex final site plan approval amid opposition on noise, water, and energy.
Also today, Lenox Township reviews its data center ordinance and possible moratorium extension.
Madison Heights City Council considers a temporary moratorium resolution.
And another planning commission reviews the new site plan for the Verrus project.
Tomorrow Ann Arbor City Planning Commission has a presentation on local impacts, policy, and zoning for Michigan communities.
Plenty of chances for residents to weigh in directly.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.
Thanks for listening.

episode_title: Michigan Data Center Tracker Maps 20+ Proposals Chasing Power Amid Rising Local Fights
